title: The eleven blessings
hookLine: sleep well, wake well, no bad dreams, dear to people and to other beings

cards: It's midnight. You're in bed, and your mind is replaying an argument from this afternoon. What you said.
What you should have said. What you'll say next time. Your heart is going a little fast.
Sleep isn't coming. The clock says twelve-forty, then one-fifteen. Today's text makes a promise that sounds surprisingly modern.
It's a short list from the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of numbered teachings, and the very first thing on it is this: a person who practices loving-kindness sleeps well.

teach.b: The text is called the Metta Sutta too, a different one, in the Book of Elevens. The Buddha lists eleven benefits for someone who practices metta often and well.

teach.h: SLEEP WELL, WAKE WELL, NO BAD DREAMS.
teach.b: One, you sleep well. Two, you wake well. Three, you don't have bad dreams.

teach.h: DEAR TO PEOPLE AND UNSEEN BEINGS.
teach.b: Five, you're dear to non-human beings, which the tradition understands as spirits and other unseen beings. Six, the gods protect you. Seven, fire, poison and weapons don't harm you.
Eight, your mind settles quickly into concentration. Nine, your face is bright and clear. Ten, you die without confusion.
And eleven, if you go no further on the path, you're reborn in a heavenly realm, the Brahma world. Different Buddhists hear a list like that in different ways.
Some take all eleven at face value, including protection from fire and weapons, and chant metta for protection.
Others hear the first few especially as plain observations: it isn't hard to see why a mind that isn't nursing grudges would sleep better, or why people warm to someone who warms to them.
The text itself doesn't explain; it lists.
But notice where it starts: not with enlightenment, not with the heavens.
With sleep, the most ordinary place in your life.

And that closes ten days of metta: four phrases, yourself, a benefactor, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, the barriers broken, all beings, the sutta, and now its blessings. Tomorrow the path turns to the breath.

how: Some Buddhists practice or chant metta before sleep, and the eleven benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya are recited in teachings and on protective chanting occasions.

games.q: it's midnight, and you're replaying an argument. what does today's practice suggest?
o: send one wish to each person from today, then yourself.
get up and check your phone.
games.why: the sutta's first promise is sleep: offer each person a wish, let them go, and end with yourself.

practice: This practice is made for bedtime, but it works now too: let the body get heavy and the breath slow, then bring to mind anyone from today, the pleasant and the difficult, one at a time, and offer each a single wish: may you be at ease.
Let each one go, like closing doors softly down a hallway. Finish with yourself: may I be at ease.

wordCard.voice: Anguttara Nikaya. The collection of numbered teachings where the Buddha lists eleven blessings for loving-kindness, starting with sleeping well.

orig.note: Pali: a benefit, a blessing; the sutta lists eleven for metta.
